author.name: Kevin White
author.tradition: Catholic/Thomistic close-reading of Aristotle; broadly continental-friendly in citing Heidegger and the phenomenological tradition in footnote 11

essay_title: The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima, III, 3-8
publication: Dialogue: Canadian Philosophical Review XXIV (1985), pp. 483-505
ocr_confidence: high; printed offprint cleanly typeset (Times-style serif) with crisp Greek transliterations; user's yellow highlighting visible throughout but does not impair text. Italics for Greek terms (phantasia, phantasma, noein, aisthesis, kinesis, nous, eide, phainomena, etc.) reliably preserved. Footnote anchors and Bekker numerals legible.
special_features: Carries no epigraph; opens directly with 'Introduction'
Eight numbered headed sections: Introduction, 1, 2 (with subsections 2.1, 2.2), 3, 4, Conclusion
92 footnotes; heavy footnote apparatus for a short article

Thomistic interpretive stance signaled obliquely: Aquinas not cited by name in the running text, but the etymological/lexical-genealogical method, the careful sequencing of soul-powers, and the appeal to St. Augustine's Confessions X.8-26 on memoria (fn. 67) align White with the Latin scholastic reception
Engages the German philological tradition (Bonitz Index Aristotelicus, Freudenthal, Wolfson) and the modern Anglophone tradition (Hicks, Ross-school, Hett's Loeb translation)

Footnote 92 — the closing bibliographical footnote — surveys the secondary literature: Frohschammer 1881, Roth 1963, Phillipe 1971, Rees 1971, Benardete 1975, Engmann 1976, Schofield 1978, Labarriere 1984

DOES cite Nussbaum: footnote 9 cites Nussbaum-Schofield 1982 edited volume on 'Saving Aristotle's Appearances'; footnote 16 cites Nussbaum's De Motu Animalium commentary on the kata metaphoran clause; footnote 63 cites Nussbaum De Motu on the einai-formulation; footnote 80 cites Nussbaum De Motu pp. 232-241 on practical phantasia in DA III.10-11 — significantly, White cites Nussbaum's 1978 first edition of De Motu without engaging her 1985 second-edition essay 'The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action,' which appeared the same year; the two essays were thus independent contemporaneous productions

section_structure.heading: Introduction
section_structure.summary: Locates DA III.3's treatment of phantasia at a critical juncture: Aristotle has just concluded sensation (II.5-III.2) and is turning to thought (nous, III.4-8), and inserts a preliminary treatment of phantasia 'since there is no thought without phantasia, just as there is no phantasia without sensation' (427b15-16). The incidental, intermediate placement signals that Aristotle treats phantasia not for its own sake but as required by the exigencies of the analysis of human thought. White announces a thematic reading of phantasia as a prelude to noein, with particular concern for its bearing on human life.

section_structure.heading: 1. Phantasia and 'Appearing'
section_structure.summary: Lexical-genealogical opening. Refuses to translate phantasia ('imagination' carries imitative, faculty-psychological, and Romantic-aesthetic connotations foreign to Aristotle). Derives the word, with Aristotle (DA III.3, 429a3-4), from phaos ('light') via phao ('to give light, shine, beam, especially of the heavenly bodies'); thence phaino ('show'), phainomai ('appear'), phantazo ('make visible'), and the verbal nouns phantasia and phantasma. Establishes the object/subject polarity in Aristotle's usage (Bonitz's species rei obiectae vs. eam actionem qua rerum imagines animo informamus; Freudenthal's Aussehen/Erscheinung vs. Vorstellung/Einbildung). White will focus exclusively on the subjective/psychological sense. Glosses Aristotle's near-tautological definition: phantasia is that in virtue of which (kath' hen) we say a phantasma comes to be in us (DA III.3, 428a1-2). Phantasma involves the transfer of an appearance from its origin in that which appears into another medium; in Aristotle's exclusive use, the soul itself is the medium into which inner appearances are cast. Background to the discussion: the Platonic-Protagorean opposition between ousia and genesis, against which Aristotle's analysis of phantasia opens.

section_structure.heading: 2. The Context of the Discussion of Phantasia
section_structure.summary: Two-subsection structuring discussion. Section 2.1 'The Plan of the De Anima' surveys the unstable architecture of De Anima books II-III: II.4 nutrition, II.5-III.2 sensation, III.3 phantasia, III.4-8 nous, III.9-11 locomotion, III.12-13 supplementary remarks on sensation. White rehearses three competing schemes for organizing III.3-11 (grades of life; the kritikon/kinetikon distinction; powers peculiar to soul vs. common to soul and body), concluding that nous is the unifying theme of III.3-11. Section 2.2 'The Introduction of De Anima, III, 3' close-reads 427a17-b14 where Aristotle distinguishes thinking (noein, phronein) from sensation, then abruptly introduces phantasia. Two sources of potential confusion between phantasia and noein are identified: (1) both can occur in the absence of a sensible object (the mnemonist arranging images at 427b18-20); (2) both can serve as inner springs of animal activity (men 'when the mind is temporarily clouded over by emotion, or disease, or sleep' act according to phantasia just as brutes do). Aristotle distinguishes them by two indications: (a) phantasia 'rests with us' as the mnemonist's images do, whereas judgment (doxazein, hypolepsis) involves reference beyond us to truth or falsity; (b) when our judgment confronts something fearful or terrible we are immediately moved, while phantasia 'coolly regards such affecting scenes as one would a picture' (427b21-24). This last is White's signature reading: the picture-vs-encounter distinction is the litmus test separating phantasia from judgment.

section_structure.heading: 3. The Definition of Phantasia
section_structure.summary: Reconstructs Aristotle's positive definition. After the introductory excursus, Aristotle aligns phantasia with aisthesis: phantasia is rooted in the act of sensation; the close resemblance is dramatically evident in dreaming, where the dreamer takes himself to be actually seeing and hearing things. But Aristotle also distinguishes them, pointedly remarking at Metaphysics IV.5, 1010b3 that phantasia is not the same as aisthesis. The decisive distinguishing point: an 'appearing' (phainetai) may occur when the sense-powers are inoperative (in dreams, with eyes closed), so phantasia cannot be sensation; yet phantasia does not occur without sensation. White then unfolds Aristotle's account of sensation as a passive 'being moved' (kineisthai), 'altered' (alloiousthai), 'acted upon' (paschein); a process of actualization (energein) involving an assimilation (homoiotai) of the sense-power to its object; the reception of sensible form without matter, like wax taking the imprint of a seal. From this account Aristotle draws the simplest and most general element — sensation is a certain physical motion (kinesis) — and uses it to define phantasia as 'a movement produced by sensation actively operating' (kinesis hypo tes aistheseos tes kat' energeian gignomenes, DA III.3, 428b10-11; 429a1-2). Phantasia is thereby specified as a secondary, derivative motion arising from sensation and continuing after the sensible object has gone and the sense-power has become inoperative. White's metaphor: phantasia is 'a reproductive faculty' through which 'the momentary, stillborn life of sensations is perpetuated in their offspring' — the sensible forms preserved freed from their original matter. The De Insomniis amplifies this with the formula that phantasia is the same as the sensitive faculty (aisthetikon) but different in einai. Phantasia is thus a dimension of the life of all animal souls, not a separate power constituting a distinct grade of life: it is sensation's after-image, the soul's storehouse of sensible forms.

section_structure.heading: 4. Phantasia and Nous
section_structure.summary: Shows how phantasia subserves the analysis of noein. Like sensation, thinking is a 'being acted upon' (paschein) which is possible because thought is receptive (dektikon) and potentially (dunamei) identical with the forms (eide) of beings (DA III.4, 429a13-18); both powers are by themselves empty, open, susceptible. The crucial difference: thought is wholly unmixed (amige) with body and matter. DA III.8 develops the parallelism: the soul is in a way all the beings (onta), aisthetika or noeta, potentially identical with their eide. Phantasia, as a modulation of the sensitive faculty integral to noein, points the way to the root unity of sensing and thinking. White then poses the central question: why does nous depend more immediately on phantasia than on aisthesis? Why are phantasmata serviceable to noein as aisthemata are not? Aristotle's answer revolves around time: aisthesis is wholly confined to 'the now' and continually withdraws each object and substitutes another, whereas phantasia 'lends to the appearances a stability which they do not have of themselves.' By preserved phantasmata, nous is enabled to continuously behold its timeless object even when the mediating sensible thing is past, absent, or in motion. Phantasia also extends nous into the future, in practical thinking (DA III.7, 431b2-10): the noetikon thinks the forms in the phantasmata, and like sense it pursues or avoids in the sphere of phantasmata. Once nous has gained a foothold in time by means of phantasia, it can put its survey of the past into the service of a calculation of the future; experience for practical wisdom rests on the preserving activity of phantasia. The geometrical analogy: phantasia is Plato's 'painter in the soul,' the noetic soul's portable slate; as a geometer uses a specific right-angled triangle to deduce a truth about all triangles, so nous, working through phantasmata, disengages the immaterial einai of material beings. Nous's dependence on phantasia thus reveals (a) thought has no memory of its own, and (b) thinking is constitutively continuous, an activity tending of its very nature 'towards a constant, uninterrupted actualization,' which the perishable human soul can only approximate through phantasia's bridging activity. The two parallel kinds of cognition (nous, aisthesis), each empty and present-directed, find their unity in the mediating retentive activity of phantasia.

section_structure.heading: Conclusion
section_structure.summary: Phantasia pervades human life. Thinking, man's highest activity, is impossible without concurrent phantasia; when the power of thought is eclipsed by emotion, disease, or sleep, man acts in accordance with phantasia just as the brutes do (DA III.3, 429a4-8). Phantasia in its hidden interaction with the passions plays a role in moral and political life (the angry, fearful, confident, shameful are described via phantasia in the Rhetoric II.2-6). Even in sleep phantasia continues, perhaps more intensely than in waking life. White's closing formula: 'man never ceases to take his bearings in the world by means of phantasia.' The lexical genealogy returns: as the roots of the word phantasia connote light, visibility, and the heavenly phenomena (Meteorologica, De Mundo, Problemata, De Coloribus), so phantasia in its objective sense names the milky way, comets, shooting stars, planets, lightning, rainbows — celestial occurrences which orient man in the cosmos. Its subjective sense imports these resonances into the inner life. White's final, distinctively Thomistic-humanist formulation: by internalizing and preserving such features, phantasia provides man with a familiar interior landscape — a faculty for the panorama of nature — which he may consult with confidence in its permanence. Its highest function is to provide an index of orientation and differentiation to nous itself. A coda points to the contemporary relevance: in our age the scene of outer appearances has been overlaid and intensified by an unprecedented proliferation of man-made phantasmata, artificial appearances formed from the beginning to become inner appearances and thereby to affect human thought, passion, and action — phantasia, paradoxically, has its greatest significance in waking and public life.

outline: Cluster 1 (PDF 1-2, book 483-484, Introduction): White situates DA III.3's introduction of phantasia at a hinge moment in the De Anima — between sensation (completed at III.2) and thought (to follow at III.4-8). Aristotle's terse statement at 427b15-16 — that there is no thought without phantasia, just as there is no phantasia without sensation — registers the complex dependency of soul-powers but introduces phantasia incidentally. White reads this incidental placement as a clue: phantasia is not treated for its own sake but because the analysis of nous, particularly human nous, requires it. The chapter on phantasia is a chapter on man, since phantasia introduces the part of the treatise that is particularly concerned with the human soul and its characteristic activity of noein.

Cluster 2 (PDF 2-3, book 484-485, §1 Phantasia and 'Appearing'): White declines to translate phantasia. 'Imagination' carries (a) the imago/imitor connotation of imitation/resemblance foreign to phantasia; (b) the later Galenic/inner-sense brain-faculty psychology; (c) the modern poetic-Romantic 'extraordinary power of insight, spiritual vision, or discovery.' He proposes to leave the word untranslated and let its meaning emerge from Aristotle's text.

Cluster 3 (PDF 3-4, book 485-486, §1 cont.): Etymological derivation. Aristotle's own derivation from phaos ('light,' DA 429a3-4) may not be strictly correct, but both words come from phao ('to give light, shine, especially of the heavenly bodies'). From phao come phaino ('show'), phainomai ('appear'), phantazo ('make visible, show oneself'), and the verbal nouns phantasia and phantasma. Genealogically, phantasia would indicate the effect of a prominent or merely noticeable self-presentation to eyesight, but it quickly acquired the wider meaning of 'a presentation to consciousness, whether immediate or in memory, whether true or illusory.' The array of all such appearances forms the scene of the pre-philosophic dimension of human experience.

Cluster 4 (PDF 4, book 486, §1 cont.): The object/subject polarity. White invokes Bonitz's Index Aristotelicus distinction between species rei obiectae (the 'look' of the thing) and eam actionem qua rerum imagines animo informamus (the action of the soul). Freudenthal's parallel: Aussehen/Erscheinung vs. Vorstellung/Einbildung. White restricts his analysis to the psychological/subjective sense — the action by which the soul presents something to itself — and so to the special kind of appearances Aristotle calls phantasmata.

Cluster 5 (PDF 5, book 487, §1 cont.): Aristotle's near-tautological definition at DA III.3, 428a1-2 (kath' hen legomen phantasma ti hemin gignesthai): phantasia is that in virtue of which we say a phantasma comes to be in us. White unpacks: (a) Aristotle describes phantasia by the ordinary way of speaking; (b) phantasia is made to account for the genesis of phantasma; (c) phantasma involves the transfer of an appearance from its origin in that which appears into another medium. In Plato, phantasmata include outer reflections (in water); in Aristotle, phantasmata are reserved for inner appearances, where we ourselves are the medium into which the reflected appearances are cast, transformed, and separated from their originals. The inner appearance becomes wholly interiorized — present only to and contained only by the individual. The kath' hen formula (Met. V.18, 1022a19-20: cause), signals that phantasia is an underlying causal action of the soul accounting for the presence in us of phantasmata.

Cluster 6 (PDF 6-9, book 488-491, §2.1 Plan of the De Anima): White surveys the architecture of De Anima books II-III. The DA's remarks on phantasia prior to III.3 are few and fragmentary (I.1, 403a8-10; II.2, 413b22-23; II.3, 414b16; III.8, 420b29-33; III.2, 425b24-25): thinking is intimately related to phantasia; phantasia along with desire is concomitant with sensation; the place of phantasia among soul-powers is unclear; some animals live according to phantasia; phantasia is somehow involved in voice; phantasiai persist in sense-organs after sense-objects have gone. The chapter on phantasia at III.3 is itself transitional between sensation (II.5-III.2) and nous (III.4-8). White rehearses competing organizational schemes for III.3-11: (a) grades-of-life; (b) the to kritikon (distinguishing power) vs. to kinetikon (locomotive power) division of III.9 432a15-17; (c) powers peculiar to soul vs. common to soul and body. He concludes that nous is the continuing and unifying theme of III.3-11.

Cluster 7 (PDF 10-12, book 492-494, §2.2 Introduction of DA III.3): Close reading of 427a17-b14. Aristotle first distinguishes thinking (noein, phronein) from sensation: neither phronein nor noein are sensation; phronein because few animals have it; noein because while sensation is always true of its proper objects and belongs to all animals, dianoeisthai may be false and belongs only to logos-having creatures. Having distinguished thinking from sensing, Aristotle abruptly introduces phantasia at 428a15-16: distinguishing it from both sensation and thought (dianoia); phantasia does not occur without sensation, nor does judgment (hypolepsis) occur without phantasia. Two sources of confusion: (a) both thinking and phantasia may occur in the absence of a sensible object (the mnemonist arranging mental images at 427b18-20); (b) both may serve as inner springs of animal activity — DA III.3, 429a4-8: 'imaginations persist in us and resemble sensations, so living creatures frequently act in accordance with them, some (brutes) because they have no mind, some (men) because the mind is temporarily clouded over by emotion, or disease, or sleep.'

Cluster 8 (PDF 12, book 494, §2.2 cont.): The picture-vs-encounter distinction at DA III.3, 427b21-24 — White's signature move. Aristotle distinguishes phantasia from judgment (doxazein) by two marks: (i) the exercise of phantasia rests with us (as in the mnemonist's images), while judging that something is the case is not so circumscribed but involves reference beyond us to truth and falsity; (ii) when our judgment confronts something fearful or terrible we are immediately moved, while phantasia 'coolly regards such affecting scenes as one would a picture.' The picture-vs-encounter distinction articulates the detachment of phantasia from the immediate practical involvement of judgment.

Cluster 9 (PDF 13-14, book 495-496, §3 Definition): Aristotle's positive definition. Phantasia is rooted in the act of sensation (aisthesis); the close resemblance is dramatically evident in the phantasia of dreaming. Yet Aristotle distinguishes them: at Metaph. IV.5, 1010b3 phantasia is not the same as aisthesis. The identification of phantasia and aisthesis is Protagorean and is rejected by both Plato and Aristotle. The decisive point distinguishing them: an 'appearing' (phainetai) may occur when the sense-powers are inoperative (in dreams or with eyes closed); yet phantasia does not occur without sensation, since both take place in the same subjects and are directed to the same objects. The precise relation between the two activities yields Aristotle's definition.

Cluster 10 (PDF 14, book 496, §3 cont.): Sensation as kinesis. Aristotle's account of aisthesis: a passive 'being moved' (kineisthai), 'altered' (alloiousthai), 'acted upon' (paschein); a process of actualization (energein) by which the passive sense-power is impinged upon by its object; an assimilation (homoiotai) in which the sense-power is transformed into a likeness of its object ('like is known by like'); the reception of sensible form without matter, like wax taking the imprint, but not the material, of a seal. Sensation is thus a physical motion, a process of actualization, an assimilation, and the reception of dematerialized form.

Cluster 11 (PDF 14, book 496, §3 cont., definition proper): The kinesis-definition. Aristotle picks out the simplest and most general element of his account of aisthesis — that it is a certain physical motion (kinesis) — and uses it to define phantasia. Observing that something moved by another may in turn move something else, and that phantasia seems to be some sort of motion depending on sensation, Aristotle defines phantasia as 'a movement produced by sensation actively operating' (kinesis hypo tes aistheseos tes kat' energeian gignomenes, 428b10-11, 429a1-2). This secondary motion necessarily resembles sensation (which is itself an assimilation to the sensible object), but continues in the absence of the sensible object and the inoperancy of the sense-power. White's metaphor: phantasia is a 'reproductive faculty' through which 'the momentary, stillborn life of sensations is perpetuated in their offspring.'

Cluster 12 (PDF 15, book 497, §3 cont.): The De Insomniis amplification. The De Insomniis 1, 459a15-22 / 3, 460b28-461a8 develops the DA account. The imaginative (phantastikon) is the same as the sensitive (aisthetikon) faculty, although different in essence (einai); phantasia is the process set up by a sense-faculty in a state of activity (he hypo tes kat' energeian aistheseos gignomene kinesis). A dream is some sort of mental image (phantasma) which appears in sleep. Dreaming belongs to the sensitive faculty, but to it qua imaginative (he phantastikon). The pathos of sensation persists after sensations have ceased (the serially-moved-projectile and alloiosis-by-transmitted-heat analogies). Aristotle's account also resembles St. Augustine's memoria (Confessions X.8-26).

Cluster 13 (PDF 16, book 498, §3 cont. closing): Phantasia is a dimension of the life of all animal souls. It is not only a receiver, but a 'preserver and storehouse' of sensible forms — the animal soul carries 'the reverberating effects of its past encounters with sensible objects.' The lingering, resonating, echoing presence of sensible forms freed from their original matter is the essence of phantasia for Aristotle.

Cluster 14 (PDF 16-17, book 498-499, §4 Phantasia and Nous): Like sensation, thinking is a 'being acted upon' (paschein), possible because thought is receptive (dektikon) and potentially (dunamei) identical with the forms (eide) of beings (DA III.4, 429a13-18). In thinking, as in sensing, cognition is not understood by means of any a priori structure other than a specific emptiness, openness, susceptibility to the forms of things. The crucial difference: thought is free of any admixture (amige) with matter and body. DA III.8 (431b21-432a1): the soul is in a way all the beings (onta); they are either sensible (aistheta) or intelligible (noeta); knowledge in a way is the knowable objects; sensation in a way is the sensible objects. The soul's two principal cognitive powers, while empty of themselves, are receptive and open to the assimilating influence of the eide of beings.

Cluster 15 (PDF 18-19, book 500-501, §4 cont., the why-of-phantasia): The central question — why does nous depend more immediately on phantasia than on aisthesis? Why are phantasmata serviceable to noein as aisthemata are not? Aristotle's answer turns on time. Aisthesis is wholly confined to 'the now' (432a3-4) and continually offers nous its object, only to at once withdraw it and substitute a different object. Even if nous could follow aisthesis through its transformations, glimpsing the essence of each in rapid succession, these would not be grasped as the unmoving or timeless einai which nous requires of its object. Phantasia 'lends to the appearances a stability which they do not have of themselves' and is the human soul's response to this dilemma. By means of preserved phantasmata, nous is enabled to continuously behold its timeless object, even when the mediating sensible thing is past, absent, or in motion. This is also why preserved phantasmata are necessary to the process of learning (Physics IV.10-14; EN X.4, 1174a13-17): without retention and accumulation of past encounters there could be no acquisition of knowledge, but only a forgetful succession of insights.

Cluster 16 (PDF 19, book 501, §4 cont.): Phantasia and the future. Beyond extending nous into the past, phantasia also extends it into the future, via the interplay of practical thinking, desire, and phantasmata (DA III.7, 431b2-10): the noetikon thinks the forms in the phantasmata; just as in sensation what is to be pursued and avoided is defined, so outside sensation, when occupied with phantasmata, the soul is moved; sometimes by the phantasmata or noemata in the soul, just as if it were seeing, it calculates and plans for the future in view of the present. Once nous has gained a foothold in time by means of phantasia, it can put its survey of the past into the service of a calculation of the future. The importance of experience for practical wisdom rests on the preserving activity of phantasia.

Cluster 17 (PDF 20, book 502, §4 cont., geometrical analogy): Aristotle's image (De Memoria 1, 449b31-450a9): it is impossible even to think (noein) without a mental picture (phantasmatos). The same affection (pathos) is involved in thinking as in drawing a diagram. The geometer draws a finite magnitude though he is not thinking of it as such. Phantasia resembles Plato's 'painter in the soul' (Philebus 39b1 ff.), whose job is to illustrate the text of the soul's grasp of truth. As a geometer with a portable slate, the noetic soul considers truth at its leisure — not because it has no need of paradigmatic sensible images, but because it can produce its own such images in the activity of phantasia. Phantasia preserves the characteristic features of sensible things, such as determinate quantity, but nous is able to disregard these and disengage the immaterial 'being' of material beings, as a geometer makes use of a specific right-angled triangle to deduce a truth about all triangles.

Cluster 18 (PDF 20-21, book 502-503, §4 cont., divided line): A discreet polemic. Aristotle's geometrical comparison may respond to Plato's divided-line account (Republic VI.510a1, e2 — VI.511d8), which compares a certain kind of thinking (dianoia) to the image-making activity of geometers. But while Socrates there describes a higher kind of thinking (noesis) which makes no use of images, Aristotle, 'like the Glaucon of the Republic,' has difficulty conceiving such pure imageless thought. Aristotle's nous is image-bound in a way Plato's is not.

Cluster 19 (PDF 21, book 503, §4 closing): Nous depends on phantasia not only for the steadiness of its object but for the continuity of its own activity. Thinking, according to Aristotle, is an activity which 'of its very nature tends towards a constant, uninterrupted actualization' (DA III.5, 430a22) and which man can perform most continuously (Nicomachean Ethics X.7, 1177a23-25). Phantasia provides some secure foundation, however intermittent, for this divine operation in the life of a perishable being. The need for phantasia thus arises from the complex way in which human cognition is related to time: phantasia prolongs the now of sensation into past and future, enabling man at certain points and for certain periods to pass beyond the confinements of sense to a consideration of the timeless natures of things. Phantasia may be both the source of the failure of human noein to fully realize itself AND what makes this activity possible at all.

Cluster 20 (PDF 21-22, book 503-504, §4 ending): Two parallel moments. Nous and aisthesis are strikingly similar in their empty receptivity and total, present-directed absorption in the forms of beings. The union of these two presents — and hence the unity of the human soul — requires the mediating activity of phantasia, which does not merely receive but retains, so that the present of sensation may be made to resemble the present of mathematics. Through phantasia, the impermanent sensible beings, in their reflections within us, are caused to imitate the fixed noeta; human thinking is thereby enabled to imitate the noetic life of the gods.

Cluster 21 (PDF 22-23, book 504-505, Conclusion): The role of phantasia in human life goes far beyond its contribution to noein and is, in fact, pervasive. Thinking, man's highest endeavor, is impossible without concurrent phantasia; when the power of thought is eclipsed (by emotion, disease, sleep) man, like brutes, acts in accordance with phantasia. Phantasia in its hidden interaction with the passions (Rhetoric II.2-6 on anger, fear, confidence, shame; De Insomniis 2 on the cowardly, erotic, angry; Rhetoric I.11 on self-image as spur to victory, honour, excellence) plays a role in moral and political life. Phantasia continues in sleep, perhaps more intensely. White's emblematic formula: 'man never ceases to take his bearings in the world by means of phantasia.'

Cluster 22 (PDF 22-23, book 504-505, Conclusion cont. — heavenly-bodies coda): Closure via the lexical genealogy. The roots of phantasia connote light, visibility, heavenly phenomena; Aristotle uses phantasia for the milky way, comets, shooting stars, planets, lightning, rainbows (Meteorologica I.3, 339a35; I.5, 342b23; II.6, 342b32; II.9, 370a15; III.4, 374b8; De Mundo 4, 395b6; Problemata XV.4, 911a13; XXVI.12, 941b22). Colours, too, each have their unique 'look' or phantasia (De Coloribus 1, 791b17; 2, 792a6, b15; 3, 793a25; Meteorologica III.2, 372b8; De Sensu 3, 439b6). These visible phenomena lend resonances to the word that carry over into its subjective meaning: as the celestial occurrences orient man in the cosmos, so the inner appearances — accompanying memory, dreaming, thinking, desire — have a 'diverting prominence in human life' parallel to the more striking features of the visible world in the panorama of nature.

Cluster 23 (PDF 23, book 505, Conclusion closing — the 'familiar interior landscape'): White's culminating formulation. By internalizing and preserving the features of the panorama of nature, the power of phantasia 'provides man with a familiar interior landscape which, in contrast with the sensible beings in themselves, he may consult with confidence in its permanence.' The relative permanence conferred on the sensible beings by phantasia is necessary and interesting to man in many practical ways, but its highest function is to provide 'an index of orientation and differentiation' to the power of nous. It is this highest function that points to the motive for the De Anima's digression on phantasia and to the deepest meaning of the inner appearances in the life of the human soul.

Cluster 24 (PDF 23, book 505, Conclusion final paragraph — contemporary coda): Aristotle's suggestions about phantasia 'would seem to be of particular relevance in our own time, when the scene of outer appearances has been overlaid and intensified by an unprecedented proliferation of man-made phantasmata.' Unlike the appearances of nature, these artificial phantasmata are in large part 'appearances of man himself,' formed from the beginning to become inner appearances and thereby to affect the course of human thought, passion, and action. Their transmission and sharing give rise to a paradox: phantasia, 'the private and inner side of man's contact with the sensible beings,' has its greatest significance in our 'waking and public life.'

concepts.label: phantasia (untranslated)
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's term for the soul-power producing inner appearances; White refuses to render it 'imagination' and lets meaning emerge from the text

concepts.label: picture-vs-encounter distinction
concepts.gloss: White's signature exegetical move: at DA III.3 427b21-24 Aristotle distinguishes phantasia from judgment by noting that when we judge fearful things we are immediately moved, while phantasia 'coolly regards such affecting scenes as one would a picture'

concepts.label: kinesis hypo tes aistheseos tes kat' energeian gignomenes
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's definition: phantasia as a movement produced by sensation actively operating (DA III.3, 428b10-11; 429a1-2)

concepts.label: phantasia as preparation for noein
concepts.gloss: White's organizing thesis: in DA III.3-8, phantasia is treated as a prelude/preparation to the analysis of nous

concepts.label: secondary motion
concepts.gloss: Phantasia as a derivative motion arising from sensation that survives the sensible object's absence

concepts.label: reproductive faculty
concepts.gloss: White's image: phantasia perpetuates the 'momentary, stillborn life of sensations' in offspring

concepts.label: preserver and storehouse of sensible forms
concepts.gloss: Phantasia's positive function: not merely a receiver but a retainer of sensible forms freed from matter

concepts.label: interior landscape
concepts.gloss: White's culminating image: phantasia provides man with a familiar interior landscape he may consult with confidence in its permanence

concepts.label: index of orientation and differentiation
concepts.gloss: Phantasia's highest function: to orient and differentiate the power of nous

concepts.label: kath' hen genesis
concepts.gloss: The kath' hen formula at DA 428a1-2 read via Met. V.18 1022a19-20 (kath' ho = aition); phantasia is the underlying causal action accounting for the presence of phantasmata in us

concepts.label: object/subject polarity of phantasia
concepts.gloss: Bonitz's species rei obiectae vs. eam actionem qua rerum imagines animo informamus; Freudenthal's Aussehen/Erscheinung vs. Vorstellung/Einbildung — the two basic senses Aristotle uses; White restricts himself to the subjective sense

concepts.label: inner appearance / interiorization
concepts.gloss: Phantasma as the inner reflection where the soul itself becomes the medium into which the reflected appearances are cast, transformed, and separated from their originals

concepts.label: ousia/genesis opposition
concepts.gloss: The Platonic-Protagorean background against which Aristotle's analysis of phantasia opens; phantasia arises in the gap between sensing and thinking, between flux and being

concepts.label: to kritikon vs. to kinetikon
concepts.gloss: The 'distinguishing power' (thought + sensation) vs. the locomotive power, the major division at DA III.9 432a15-17 that White invokes as one organizational scheme for the latter half of the DA

concepts.label: amige (unmixed) character of nous
concepts.gloss: Crucial difference from sensation: nous is free of any admixture with matter and body (DA III.4, 429a13-18; III.5, 430a17-18)

concepts.label: specific emptiness/openness/susceptibility
concepts.gloss: White's gloss on dektikon/dunamei: cognition is not understood by means of any a priori structure other than a specific emptiness, openness, and susceptibility to the forms of things

concepts.label: stability lent to appearances
concepts.gloss: Phantasia 'lends to the appearances a stability which they do not have of themselves' — the temporal solution to aisthesis's confinement to the now

concepts.label: thought has no memory
concepts.gloss: White's striking subsidiary thesis: nous of itself has no memory; retention is a function of phantasia

concepts.label: continuity of noesis
concepts.gloss: Thinking by its very nature tends toward a constant, uninterrupted actualization (DA III.5, 430a22; EN X.7, 1177a23-25); phantasia provides the foundation for this

concepts.label: geometer's portable slate
concepts.gloss: Phantasia as Plato's 'painter in the soul' (Philebus 39b ff.); the noetic soul considers truth at its leisure by producing its own paradigmatic images

concepts.label: man-made phantasmata
concepts.gloss: The contemporary coda: artificial appearances 'formed from the beginning to become inner appearances and thereby to affect the course of human thought, passion, and action'

concepts.label: panorama of nature
concepts.gloss: The cosmic-orientational scene from which phantasia derives its etymological resonance and whose features it internalizes for the human soul

readings.label: Phantasia as preparation for noein (theoretical-cognitive over practical-action reading)
readings.thesis: White's organizing thesis: phantasia in DA III.3-8 is treated by Aristotle as a preliminary, theoretical-cognitive condition for the analysis of human nous, not primarily as a faculty of practical action. White stays within III.3-8, postponing III.9-11 to footnotes.
readings.contestation: Directly contrasts with Nussbaum (1985), who argues that the action passages of DA III.9-11 and De Motu Animalium are 'just as valuable evidence' and that prior scholarship was 'one-sided' in privileging DA III.3 + Parva Naturalia. White's confinement to III.3-8 is the methodological mirror-image of Nussbaum's expansion to III.9-11.

readings.label: Picture-vs-encounter distinction as litmus separating phantasia from judgment
readings.thesis: At DA III.3 427b21-24 Aristotle marks phantasia off from judgment by the detachment-from-immediate-affect criterion: judgment of something fearful moves us immediately, while phantasia 'coolly regards such affecting scenes as one would a picture.' White treats this as the decisive criterion of phantasia's distinctness.
readings.contestation: This reading is in tension with Nussbaum's reading of phantasia as the 'seeing-as' that supplies the object of desire and motivates action — for Nussbaum the immediacy of practical phantasia is constitutive, not bracketed.

readings.label: Phantasia as the temporal mediator that gives nous a foothold in time
readings.thesis: Phantasia 'lends to the appearances a stability which they do not have of themselves' (cf. DA III.4-8) by preserving sensible forms past the now of aisthesis; nous's timeless object thereby gains a steady substrate, and nous gains both retention (memory of past) and projection (calculation of future).
readings.contestation: Compatible with but more time-philosophically articulated than Nussbaum's account; the temporal-mediation thesis is the deeper continental-friendly Heideggerian undercurrent of White's reading.

readings.label: Reproductive-faculty metaphor: phantasia perpetuates sensation in 'offspring'
readings.thesis: Phantasia, as the power whereby sensation generates a likeness of itself that survives it, is to be 'likened to a reproductive faculty: through it, the momentary, stillborn life of sensations is perpetuated in their offspring.' This biological metaphor reframes the kinesis-definition.
readings.contestation: Original to White; not paralleled in Nussbaum, who uses the seeing-as/Wittgensteinian register rather than biological-generative imagery.

readings.label: Interior-landscape thesis: phantasia provides a permanent familiar inner world
readings.thesis: By internalizing and preserving the features of the panorama of nature, phantasia provides man with 'a familiar interior landscape which, in contrast with the sensible beings in themselves, he may consult with confidence in its permanence.' Its highest function is to be 'an index of orientation and differentiation' to nous.
readings.contestation: This is the Thomistic-humanist culmination distinctive to White; it has no analogue in Nussbaum, whose closing formulations are about 'how the world looks to the creature' as the ground of action explanation, not about an interior landscape of stable confidence.

readings.label: Phantasia mediates the unity of nous and aisthesis in the human soul
readings.thesis: Nous and aisthesis are strikingly similar in their empty receptivity and present-directed absorption, but they are otherwise disjoined (the fleeting present of sensation vs. the abiding present of mathematical truth). Phantasia is the soul's response to this disjunction, retaining what aisthesis only receives so that one present may be made to resemble the other.
readings.contestation: Compatible with Nussbaum's two-description ('different in einai') reading of the phantasia-aisthesis relation but more strongly metaphysical and time-philosophical in framing.

readings.label: Contemporary-relevance coda: man-made phantasmata in our age
readings.thesis: Aristotle's account is especially relevant to our time because the outer scene has been 'overlaid and intensified by an unprecedented proliferation of man-made phantasmata' — artificial appearances designed from the start to become inner appearances; phantasia thereby has its greatest significance in waking and public life.
readings.contestation: Original cultural-philosophical move; Nussbaum has no analogue.

tensions.label: Phantasia as theoretical-cognitive vs. practical-motivational
tensions.description: White confines his exegesis to DA III.3-8 and treats phantasia primarily as preparation for noein, mentioning practical phantasia (DA III.9-11, De Motu) only in footnote 80. This is the methodological inverse of Nussbaum's expansion of phantasia into action-explanation. The cluster as a whole turns on which textual loci should govern interpretation.

tensions.label: Picture-vs-encounter detachment vs. interpretive-immediacy
tensions.description: The picture-vs-encounter distinction (427b21-24) — phantasia 'coolly regards' affecting scenes — emphasizes detachment from immediate practical involvement. This pulls against the Nussbaum-style reading where phantasia is the 'seeing-as' that supplies the desired object and motivates action. The tension is internal to Aristotle's text and runs through the cluster.

tensions.label: Source of nous's failure / source of nous's possibility
tensions.description: White's striking dialectical formulation: phantasia 'may be the source of the failure of human noein to fully realize itself, but it is also what makes this activity possible at all.' Phantasia is both finitizing (it binds nous to images, to time, to perishability) and enabling (it gives nous a foothold in time, retention, continuity).

tensions.label: Phantasia/aisthesis 'same but different in einai'
tensions.description: The famously perplexing formulation at DA III.3 / De Insomniis 1 — phantasia and aisthesis are activities of the same subject with the same organic foundation but differ in einai. White, like Nussbaum, finds this formulation difficult, but reads it via the secondary-motion-arising-from-primary-motion analogy rather than via Nussbaum's two-description (arete/dikaiosune) parsing.

tensions.label: Natural phantasmata vs. man-made phantasmata
tensions.description: Closing coda raises a contemporary tension: artificial phantasmata (mass-mediated images) are deliberately fashioned to become inner appearances and so to affect human thought, passion, and action. This inverts the natural direction of phantasia-formation (from outer panorama to inner landscape) and gives phantasia, paradoxically, its greatest weight in public life.

tensions.label: Phantasia divides man between present and past
tensions.description: 'The difference between present sensation and the present persistence of past sensation seems to be a kind of tension, potentially dividing man between his present and his past, between what confronts him in the world and what preoccupies him within.' Phantasia is both the unifier of the temporal soul and the agent of its inner self-division.

nussbaum_comparison: White and Nussbaum publish in the same year (1985) on the same theme (Aristotle's phantasia) but produce essentially independent essays: White cites Nussbaum's 1978 first-edition De Motu Animalium commentary (fns. 16, 63, 80), not her 1985 reframed essay 'The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action,' and Nussbaum's footnote 71 acknowledges only Schofield. The two essays are methodologically mirror-images. NUSSBAUM expands the textual base FROM DA III.3 + Parva Naturalia TO DA III.9-11 + De Motu, arguing that prior scholarship has been 'one-sided.' WHITE deliberately restricts himself TO DA III.3-8 and treats III.9-11 only in footnote 80, with phantasia framed as preparation for noein. They CONVERGE on (i) the lexical-genealogical priority of phainetai/phainomena over the imago/imitor connotation of 'imagination,' (ii) reading the kath' hen formula at 428a1-2 as the central definition, (iii) recognizing the einai-formulation (DA 459a15-22) as the crux of the phantasia/aisthesis relation, (iv) finding the kata metaphoran clause more limited in scope than the imagistic reading requires, and (v) endorsing DA III.8 432a3-10 ('the soul never thinks without a phantasma') as a substantive claim about thinking. They DIVERGE on (i) which textual base should govern interpretation — III.3-8 for White, III.9-11 + MA for Nussbaum; (ii) the picture-vs-encounter passage 427b21-24, which is decisive for White and barely mentioned by Nussbaum (whose 'seeing-as' reading effaces White's detachment-criterion); (iii) the einai-formulation, which White reads via secondary-motion-from-primary-motion physics whereas Nussbaum reads via the road-up/road-down / arete-dikaiosune analogies as 'two descriptions of one capacity'; (iv) the systematic role of phantasia, which White makes the temporal-mediating substrate of noein and Nussbaum makes the interpretive 'how things appear' that motivates desire and action; (v) the philosophical horizon — White's interior-landscape culmination is Thomistic-humanist, while Nussbaum's seeing-as conclusion is Wittgensteinian-Anglophone analytic. The two essays are most usefully read as the theoretical-cognitive (White) and the practical-motivational (Nussbaum) limbs of a complete 1985 reassessment, mutually illuminating where they touch the same Bekker passages.
